explanation: No single trigger. The top examples are a grab-bag: chart type 'line', the boost 'units' path, 'Terms and Conditions', a subword of 'radionuclides', 'template<>', Go 'import (', and street-address words ('St', 'Ave', 'Street'). Mid and weak activations are scattered too. Hard to predict beyond street-address names and legal/code boilerplate fragments giving moderate-to-strong activation.

Fires on the last subword piece that completes a rare, multi-token proper name or alphanumeric identifier: the final digit of a price or model number (1,209.99, U-937, BMP180, 40,000, 1967) or the end of a foreign or unusual name (Torvalds, Babruysk, Khaleda, Jabodetabek, Kyaw). The token itself matters less than finishing such a name or number. Ordinary words and punctuation give at most weak activation.

Leans toward content words in technical Q&A posts (e.g. 'Windows', 'app', 'save', 'eclipse', 'IE' after 'Q: How to...'), Objective-C alloc brackets and stack-trace 'from'. It also fires strongly on unrelated tokens: a football score '0-0', 'send our thoughts', dental 'dentin'/'resin' and the DTD doctype. A loose mixture centred on programming help questions.

Two unrelated jobs. (1) Modal or auxiliary verbs right after a subject, as in 'Any help will be...', 'Any answer would be appreciated', 'it will be useful', 'nothing could', 'a bullet may'. (2) Inner subword pieces of foreign personal or religious names (Bartol-ome-o, Bh-ag-avatha, Naz-are-ne, Madhub-ala, Matte-o). A few HTML charset meta tokens also fire.

Fires on tokens inside software license and copyright header boilerplate at the top of source files: 'Copyright ... Authors', 'you may not use this file', 'WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY', 'sublicense, and/or sell', indentation before the Apache URL. Legal headers such as 'COURT OF APPEALS' and the SQL 'You have an error' message also fire. Strength depends on being in that boilerplate context, not on the token itself.

Hard to characterise. It often fires near the start of a document or intro sentence, on commas separating list items (cities, firms, 'friends, family') and on function or connective words ('or', 'a', 'and', 'to', 'the latest', 'brought'). It also fires on JSON/XML keys like 'tools'. There is no clear unifying feature.

Fires on the first subword fragment of a word that is split into several tokens and must continue. This is mostly non-English text (Dutch 'felbegeerde', German 'zurück', French, Romanian, Portuguese, Spanish) and place names (Kanagawa, Trieste, Balochistan, Mecca, Roraima), plus Latinate medical words (vertebrae, contralateral, spurs). Whole common English words are weak.

Fires on word-internal subword pieces of rare words: Latin or medical terms (orbicularis, transesophageal, ejection, pre-eclampsia, Populus), foreign names (Garcia, Giacomo, Brjánsdóttir, Famalicão) and non-English text (Indonesian 'jalur', Czech, French). Activation is modest except the top example. Common words and punctuation are near zero.

The single top example is a number in a math word problem. Other activations are moderate and spread over math notation (lim, sin, partition function, polynomials), diabetes and insulin vocabulary (beta-cell, insulin), code tokens (NSError **, ports) and random phrases. A mixture with weak math and biomedical leanings.

Fires on subword pieces inside words in non-English, especially morphologically rich, languages: Hungarian ('szolgáltatás'), Russian, Czech, Finnish, Turkish suffixes, and German compound parts ('Daten-bank', 'An-zahl'). The strongest cases are word-internal pieces in Hungarian or Cyrillic text. English text gives almost nothing.

Mostly punctuation or syntax tokens inside technical strings: LaTeX braces ('}{'), shell/sed/awk symbols ('&', 'backslash-semicolon', '|', '}'), URL path segments ('/group', '/android', '.com', '/services'), Python '(*' and Apache config braces. There are also scattered prose cases like 'tip of' an island and petrol bombs. Moderate activations overall.

Mixed. It fires on modals after negation or subject ('Nothing could', 'we can'), on 'WARRANTIES' in license text, and on nouns that complete a noun phrase after a modifier or determiner ('poor egg quality', 'gross income', 'revenue growth', 'our bodies', 'skin diseases'). It also fires on SQLSTATE and 'thread' in error messages. No clear single concept.

Strongest on individual CJK characters in Chinese or Japanese text. Separately, it fires moderately on function words and sentence-final periods in English license boilerplate ('redistribute it and/or', 'continuing to use', 'file in') and academic prose ('two types of information.'). These look like unrelated jobs.

No coherent pattern. Strong activations fall on final subwords of personal names (Shardha, Dumervil, Dillashaw, Gudnason), newlines in code or license headers, 'and/or' in Oracle copyright, '[the' in markdown, and assorted function words or commas in prose. Unpredictable beyond a loose preference for name-ending subwords.
